defaults.permitted_development: Across Oxfordshire, a simple skylight or roof-light is commonly permitted development provided it remains a minor roof alteration, projects no more than 150mm from the slope and does not exceed the roof's existing height. Heritage controls, local restrictions and larger roof changes can all take the work outside that simpler route.

rules.height_rules: Across Oxfordshire, a roof-light must not push the roof above the existing highest part. Keeping the frame low-profile and subordinate to the roof slope is usually the safest approach.
rules.depth_rules: Across Oxfordshire, projection is one of the key measurable limits: no more than 150mm from the existing roof plane. If the proposal is too bulky, it can move out of the simple roof-light category and into a fuller planning assessment.
rules.boundary_rules: Across Oxfordshire, the main boundary issue for roof-lights is overlooking. Where the opening is side-facing, obscure glazing and a 1.7 metre minimum height to any opening part are the usual safeguards under the householder route.
rules.roof_rules: Across Oxfordshire, think of a roof-light as a small insertion into the existing slope, not as a way to reshape the roof. Larger additions, terraces and platforms are outside the ordinary roof-light allowance.
rules.materials_rules: Across Oxfordshire, choose a roof-light that feels recessive rather than attention-seeking. Simple frame colours, tidy flashings and detailing that works with the existing roof covering generally give the strongest planning outcome.

restrictions.conservation_area: In conservation areas, even small roof-lights can need closer scrutiny if they are proposed on prominent slopes or on buildings with a consistent historic roofscape.
restrictions.listed_building: Listed building consent may be required for roof-lights where the work alters historic roof fabric, framing, coverings or the character of the building.
restrictions.article4_notes: Roof-specific planning conditions and Article 4 directions are a common reason why an otherwise modest roof-light still needs planning permission.

rules.permitted_development: In Oxford, a simple skylight or roof-light is commonly permitted development provided it remains a minor roof alteration, projects no more than 150mm from the slope and does not exceed the roof's existing height. Heritage controls, local restrictions and larger roof changes can all take the work outside that simpler route.

rules.height_rules: The roof-light should not make any part of the roof higher than it is now. A low-profile installation that leaves the original roof form dominant is generally the strongest option.
rules.depth_rules: Projection is one of the key measurable limits: no more than 150mm from the existing roof plane. If the proposal is too bulky, it can move out of the simple roof-light category and into a fuller planning assessment.
rules.boundary_rules: Boundary impact usually comes through privacy rather than distance. Side-facing roof-light windows should be obscure-glazed and, if openable, the opening part should have its lowest point at least 1.7 metres above the room floor.
rules.roof_rules: Think of a roof-light as a small insertion into the existing slope, not as a way to reshape the roof. Larger additions, terraces and platforms are outside the ordinary roof-light allowance.
rules.materials_rules: The best material strategy is usually visual restraint. Low-profile frames and clean flashings that work with the existing roof covering are less likely to jar with the roofscape than chunky or highly contrasting units.

restrictions.conservation_area: A roof-light in a conservation area is usually easiest to justify when it is discreetly placed and does not disrupt an established roof form.
restrictions.listed_building: Roof-lights in listed buildings are commonly treated as heritage works because the roof covering, structure and external appearance all contribute to significance.
restrictions.article4_notes: A local Article 4 direction or earlier planning condition can take away the normal roof-light permitted development route, particularly on prominent roof slopes.

rules.permitted_development: In Vale of White Horse, roof-lights are often permitted development where they stay low-profile, project no more than 150mm from the roof plane and do not rise above the existing roof height. The straightforward route can disappear if the property is listed, subject to local restrictions or if the proposal starts to read as a roof enlargement rather than a simple skylight.

rules.height_rules: The alteration must not exceed the height of the existing roof. In practice that means choosing a low-profile unit that sits quietly within the roof slope rather than reading as an added structure on top of it.

rules.materials_rules: Materials are not just about weathering: they control how visible the roof-light looks. Neat flashings, restrained frame colours and a low-profile unit usually sit better than bright trims or bulky cassettes.

restrictions.conservation_area: Roof-lights on prominent roof slopes in conservation areas often face a closer design review, especially where they would affect a traditional roofscape or visible frontage.
restrictions.listed_building: A listed building roof usually needs a heritage-led approach: even a small roof-light can require consent if it affects the historic fabric or appearance.
